nicheStories.title: Aiming at the Gulf, Iran shoots itself in the foot
nicheStories.description: For decades, Iran has sought to diminish America’s military presence and political influence in the Middle East. Yet some ambitions carry within them the seeds of their own undoing. The very policies intended to push out the United States have instead strengthened the rationale for Washington’s continued engagement.Before the erosion of its regional axis, Iran based its security doctrine on forward defense, projecting influence beyond its borders to keep threats at bay. However, what Tehran regarded as a defensive strategy, the Persian Gulf states perceived as an expansionist bid for regional primacy. As a result, they deepened their security ties with Washington, making the U.S. military presence more indispensable to Gulf security rather than less.Iran’s current approach suggests that it is repeating the same strategic mistake, both in its confrontation with the United States and in its vision for the regional order that will follow.Iran’s strategy of targeting Gulf states, which Tehran views as facilitating U.S. military operations, appears intended to demonstrate that the American presence is a liability rather than an asset. The objective is to persuade Gulf leaders that hosting U.S. bases brings greater insecurity and that accommodation with Iran is a safer alternative. Yet, given the history of Iranian coercion and the prevailing lack of trust, these states are more likely to conclude that accommodating Iran would invite further pressure rather than reduce it, much as Iran itself has come to believe that restraint toward the United States invites further attacks.Iran appears to overlook one of the most enduring patterns in international politics. States facing rising security threats rarely respond by distancing themselves from their security partners. More often, they reinforce existing alliances. The United Arab Emirates moved toward the Abraham Accords amid growing concerns about Iranian regional influence and again sought Israel’s help during Iranian attacks this year. Likewise, despite being attacked by multiple actors during the recent regional conflict, Qatar neither distanced itself from the United States nor moved closer to Iran. Instead, it sought stronger American security guarantees.At the same time, Iran seeks to convey that the United States can no longer protect its regional partners. Through its relatively successful targeted attacks across the Gulf, Tehran aims to show that the U.S. security umbrella can be penetrated. Yet this strategy also overlooks the Gulf’s limited strategic alternatives. Although some Gulf states have expanded their engagement with China, Beijing currently lacks both the capability and the intent to provide security guarantees comparable to those of the United States. Nor are Gulf states likely to seek protection from a country that is itself threatening them. Consequently, rather than diminishing America’s relevance, Iranian coercion has made Washington appear increasingly indispensable because no other external power can match its military infrastructure, intelligence capabilities, or ability to project force across the Gulf.Iran should also pay closer attention to the evolving U.S. National Security Strategy during President Donald Trump’s second term in office. Washington’s long-term priorities are gradually shifting away from the Middle East and toward theaters where sustained strategic competition is expected to define American grand strategy. Accordingly, the United States seeks to reduce its direct burden in the Middle East while allowing regional states greater responsibility for shaping a stable order. Yet, instead of positioning itself within that emerging order, Iran appears intent on constructing one centered on its own regional primacy. In doing so, it only increases the likelihood of continued American involvement or support for a competing regional order designed to balance against Iran.The same dynamic has undermined another key Iranian objective. Iran has long hoped that opposition to Israel would foster greater political convergence across the region. Yet it is precisely Tehran’s regional overreach that has hindered broader Arab convergence behind the Palestinian cause, which remains fundamentally an Arab issue. Indeed, had Iran not pursued an expansive regional project, the Palestinian cause might have attracted broader regional support.The reason is straightforward. As long as Gulf leaders continue to view Iran itself as a source of regional instability, they are unlikely to subordinate their security concerns to broader Arab solidarity. Ironically, a strategy intended to strengthen resistance against Israel has instead encouraged closer security coordination against Iran.Iran no longer needs to prove it has regional influence. It has already demonstrated its ability to survive a combined U.S.-Israeli onslaught and to project power across the Middle East. Its influence in neighboring states, including Lebanon and Yemen, and its ability to affect maritime security around the Strait of Hormuz are already well understood. Iran does not need to establish hegemony over the Strait of Hormuz to demonstrate that it retains the capability to threaten its closure. Continuing to emphasize these capabilities through repeated coercive signaling, therefore, offers diminishing strategic returns and yields the opposite outcomes.Power seldom commands enduring respect through its perpetual display; for what is ceaselessly wielded soon teaches others not submission, but preparation.The future of Pakistan-Iran relations also hinges on Iran’s approach to the Gulf. Islamabad has begun to play a larger role in Gulf security. Pakistan signed the Strategic Mutual Defense Agreement (SMDA) with Saudi Arabia last year and is exploring deeper security ties with the other Middle Eastern states, including Kuwait.This evolving regional architecture presents Tehran with an important strategic choice. If Iran continues to rely on pressure against the Gulf monarchies, it risks placing Pakistan in an increasingly difficult position. Islamabad seeks constructive relations with Tehran. However, Pakistan wants not only to maintain but also to deepen strategic partnerships with Gulf states. Should Iranian pressure on the Gulf intensify, Pakistan may eventually be drawn more firmly into a regional security framework designed to reassure its Gulf partners. Continued Iranian pressure could also gradually shift Pakistani public opinion against Iran. Such an outcome would serve neither country’s long-term interests. Iran should, therefore, not assume that Pakistan’s defense commitments lack a firm basis, nor should it create circumstances that compel Islamabad to test those commitments.A more flexible approach would not require Iran to abandon its national interests or weaken its defensive posture. It would simply require recognizing that integration into regional economic and security infrastructure would serve its long-term interests. The Gulf states increasingly regard economic diversification, regional connectivity, and political stability as central to their national priorities. Iran also faces significant economic challenges after years of sanctions and the war. These shared interests provide a stronger foundation for regional order than coercion could ever offer.If Tehran genuinely seeks a Middle East that is less dependent on outside powers and more capable of managing its own affairs, it should seize the current diplomatic opening and map out a strategy built on reassurance and integration rather than coercive leverage. Such an approach would pay off not only for Gulf stability but also for Iran’s own strategic interests.Iran should move beyond seeking popular sympathy among Arab populations and instead forge lasting partnerships with regional states. It should set aside its ideological lens in favor of greater pragmatism and work toward ending its regional isolation. Rather than intimidating its neighbors, Iran should pursue cooperation based on a model of shared prosperity.

nicheStories.title: Violence in Mali is pushing Mauritania to the brink
nicheStories.description:
Mauritania, once considered a counterterrorism success story, sits at the edge of escalating violence. In the last year, Jamaat Nusrat al Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM), al-Qaeda’s affiliate in the Sahel, has expanded its operational presence in towns and villages along Mauritania’s southeastern border. But, according to locals, the most immediate threat to the country’s stability comes from its neighbor, Mali.On April 25, coordinated attacks rocked Mali, exposing the limits of state control there. Terrorists and separatist rebels targeted multiple cities, including the capital, assassinating the defense minister and prompting Malian forces and Russian Africa Corps paramilitary forces to withdraw from key northern bases. Then, on July 4, rebels launched a second, smaller offensive, targeting central and northern cities, demonstrating their resolve and operational sophistication. As the situation spirals, the United States is weighing airstrikes against JNIM militants, according to the Washington Post.The conflict in Mali is no longer contained within its borders. Refugee flows, cross-border military operations, and deteriorating relations between Bamako and Nouakchott are putting new pressures on Mauritania, particularly in vulnerable border regions. Left unchecked, these tensions could erode the security gains that Mauritania has maintained for more than a decade.Mauritania’s fragile stabilityMauritania is distinguished by its relative stability in a volatile region; the country has not experienced a terrorist attack in nearly 15 years.
The official narrative is that Nouakchott combined military operations with programs that promote moderation, including some that invited imams to preach tolerance to imprisoned terrorists. The country has “deconstructed extremist discourse,” said a former minister during an interview this spring. Others claim Mauritania reached an understanding with al-Qaeda affiliates, citing documents seized during the raid that killed Osama Bin Laden. 
As security improved in Mauritania, its neighbor, Mali, became embroiled in a series of crises. In 2012, advancing Tuareg rebels seemed poised to collapse the state, prompting France to deploy its forces to halt the offensive. Confronted by intense military pressure, some rebel factions began collaborating with al-Qaeda-affiliated groups, ultimately giving rise to an indigenous, and increasingly entrenched, terrorist presence. As of February, more than 300,000 refugees from Mali had fled to Mauritania, straining the state’s resources. 
The situation along the border is complicated, to say the least. Mauritanians are concerned about the influx of Malian refugees, who some local officials estimate arrive in the east at a rate of “hundreds per day” during an interview with the author this spring. Malians, on the other hand, are suspicious of Mauritania, which they accuse of serving as a rear base for terrorists after Nouakchott reportedly sealed a non-aggression pact with regional al-Qaeda affiliates. 
At the same time, strong transborder ties connect the two countries. Border communities have familial and financial relations in both countries. Commercial routes run along the more than 1,000-mile border. Roughly 70% of Mauritanian livestock graze in Mali annually. Along the border, economic interdependence has historically transcended politics and security crises. Rising tensions along the borderBut Malian forces, alongside the Kremlin-backed Africa Corps, stand accused of killing scores of Mauritanian herders since the seasonal migration began in January. Local officials in Mauritania’s Guidimakha region report at least a dozen disappearances since then, leaving relatives uncertain of their fate. Despite government warnings, herders continue to cross into Mali, a necessity in a country where livestock accounts for roughly 10% of GDP.This is an inversion of expected dynamics: herders can transit through terrorist-controlled areas but experience violence in areas under Bamako’s “control.” With terrorists, they are able to negotiate in-kind payments in exchange for safe passage through a region or access to pasture land therein. It is primarily in state-controlled areas where herders are targeted and, by some accounts, killed.Malian operations have also reportedly crossed into Mauritanian territory, targeting border villages like Melga and Gogui. In border regions, locals now argue that Malian and Africa Corps operations are the primary source of instability. “When [terrorists] cross the border, they leave their arms behind… When the Malian military came, they were armed to the teeth. I pray that they do not come again,” said the mayor of a town that experienced such an incursion.Security sources can recount at least six incidents in which Malian patrols crossed into Mauritanian villages this year, and the state’s response has left some citizens frustrated. Mauritania’s denials that the incursions occurred within its territory prompted a member of parliament to rhetorically question whether his district was considered part of Mali. Residents of affected villages insist they are Mauritanian, with Mauritanian schools and government offices.During an audience with President Mohamed Ould El Ghazouani earlier this year, Mauritanians living along the border urged the state to attack Mali or at least secure grazing rights. But there are no easy solutions to this problem. Escalation risks conflict, while restraint could result in more cross-border incursions. According to a member of parliament, Ghazouani said during a private meeting with the opposition in April that tensions with Mali were his greatest concern.Malian instability as regional riskThe deepening insecurity in Mali is accelerating an already fragile situation. The Malian military’s shortcomings were on full display in late April, when a terrorist and rebel onslaught put them on the backfoot nationwide. They have repeatedly failed to defend population centers from attacks, demonstrating how precarious their effective control of territory is.
That leaves Mauritanians vulnerable. “The Malian military kills because it cannot distinguish between friend and foe,” according to a local researcher. Mauritanian herders probably will continue to find themselves in the crosshairs of counterterrorism operations as conditions on the ground deteriorate. 
Diplomacy has failed to end the problem. The Malian military junta has alienated itself from other neighboring states, including Algeria and Côte d’Ivoire, and now appear intent on doing the same with Mauritania. The present turmoil makes renewed diplomacy more difficult. “We have no partner in Bamako, where the regime is living the last days of its power,” said a Mauritanian opposition politician during an interview with the author. Preventing a wider crisisAs security deteriorates and JNIM attempts to position itself as an alternative to the Malian state, the Malian military’s attacks against Mauritanians could prove dangerous. Herders, whose livelihoods depend on cross-border mobility, face mounting insecurity with few options for redress. Locals warn that these pressures could drive some toward “alliances” with terrorists.
Mali’s actions, intended to project force and security, could inadvertently generate the very grievances and vulnerabilities that sustain terrorist movements. The region is already home to one of the world’s most powerful al-Qaeda affiliates. A more entrenched JNIM, with access to a larger pool of sympathizers or potential recruits, would threaten both Mali and its neighbors. In a worst-case scenario, cooperation between Mauritanian herders and JNIM in southern Mali could prove fatal to the Mauritanian model, ending 15 years of relative security in the country.The conflict’s spread beyond Mali’s borders has proved disastrous for regional security. In 2025, the Global Terrorism Index ranked Burkina Faso, which neighbors Mali, as the country most affected by terrorism for the third consecutive year. JNIM attacked a military airbase in Niger’s capital city earlier this month.
As conflict expands, U.S. leaders are sounding the alarm. In late May, the U.S. AFRICOM Commander called West Africa “an intelligence black hole” and testified that terrorists in the region threatened U.S. personnel, facilities, and interests. A JNIM presence in Mauritania would complicate the intelligence picture and exacerbate the problem. 
Washington should monitor the situation, though it is ultimately Mali and Mauritania’s to resolve. This would require sustained engagement and a return to regular dialogue. The two states could rely on the Mali-Mauritania Joint Interministerial Commission or revive a more technical commission for border demarcation to help reduce misunderstandings in remote areas where civilians, soldiers, and militants are in close proximity. Equally important, Bamako should make an effort to demonstrate greater restraint during counterterrorism operations, and Nouakchott should remain open to dialogue if it wishes to address Malian distrust and suspicion. 
Mauritania and Mali cannot change their geography, nor the border communities and economies that bind them. As insecurity proliferates, it has become evident that only a coordinated, cross-border approach can prevent local tensions from evolving into a broader regional crisis.

nicheStories.title: Could Trump really invade Cuba?
nicheStories.description: CBS News reported recently that Pentagon officials were exploring the possibility of military action against Cuba.“Military planners have in recent weeks examined a range of options for possible action against the island, including an Army-led air assault involving thousands of U.S. soldiers to be carried out by the 101st Airborne Division, the only unit trained for such a task,” according to the report.Only days later, the State Department released a 100-page report describing Cuba as a “unique threat” to U.S. national security, claiming Havana sought to “turn America against itself” and even “conquer” the United States. Some analysts and commentators interpreted the report as an effort to lay the political groundwork for possible military action.President Donald Trump has also repeatedly declared that he intends to overthrow Cuba's government, at one point saying that he might “stop by” the island after he was “finished” with the war in Iran.Experts who spoke with Responsible Statecraft cautioned that reports of military planning should not necessarily be interpreted as evidence that an intervention is imminent. Several said the recent rhetoric and reported contingency planning could just as easily reflect an effort to increase pressure on Havana. Should Washington ultimately decide to use force, they warned, any operation aimed at toppling the Cuban government would confront far greater military, political, and humanitarian risks than the administration's rhetoric suggests.Those risks extend well beyond the immediate military operation. A war in Cuba could trigger a migration crisis just 90 miles from Florida, create opportunities for other armed groups to exploit instability, and lead to a prolonged U.S. military occupation.While the recent CBS News report points to an "Army-led air assault" as one plausible scenario, what military action against Cuba might actually look like remains unclear. The administration could intensify pressure through a blockade; pursue an air campaign or decapitation strike intended to weaken the regime without occupying the island; or launch a ground invasion.Which path the administration ultimately pursues may depend largely on Washington's political objective. The more limited options could increase pressure on Havana but may prove insufficient if the goal is to overthrow the Cuban government. Yet the option most likely to achieve that objective — a ground invasion — is also the one experts who spoke with RS considered the least likely because of its enormous costs.The reports come amid a continuing humanitarian crisis on the island. Cuba has been under a de facto oil embargo since February, leaving the country victim to regular fuel shortages and blackouts.Mark Cancian, senior adviser at the Defense and Security Department at the Center for Strategic and International studies, says a continued blockade continues to be the most probable outcome. "It puts the regime under permanent pressure," Cancian, a retired Marine Corps Colonel, told RS. "But it can't force the regime to change."Lee Schlenker, a research associate with the Global South program at the Quincy Institute, said the potential blowback is one reason he remains skeptical that the administration is preparing to invade. The U.S. may not “need to use military tools because the economic warfare has been so devastatingly effective," Schlenker, who recently visited the island, told RS. At the same time, he added, the current approach may not be enough to force the government out. “I think history has shown and the Cuban government has been very clear that the more you pressure them, the more you back them into a corner, the more you produce the siege mentality ,” Schlenker said. “They'll just continue to close ranks.”Should the administration conclude that economic and maritime pressure had failed, analysts say a limited air campaign would represent the next rung on the escalation ladder. Rather than immediately launching a broad bombing campaign, planners would more likely focus on narrowly defined military objectives including suppressing Cuban air defenses, striking military infrastructure, or targeting intelligence facilities, Cancian said.Recent American military operations have demonstrated the limits of so-called decapitation strikes. “The first day of the Iran war was like the purest example of a decapitation strike,” Dan Grazier, Director of the National Security Reform Program at the Stimson Center, told RS, referencing the killing of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. “This is the very essence of air power doctrine. You drop bombs in a very strategic fashion, trying to upend the whole enemy system.” Despite that tactical success, the war in Iran is still going nearly five months later. Grazier added that the Trump administration should avoid drawing broad conclusions from its January operation in Venezuela, saying that the special forces operation to remove President Nicolas Maduro “could have gone sideways very easily.”And, having seen the Venezuela operation, the regime in Cuba may also be better prepared for such an eventuality. “There's always an element of luck,” Cancian said. “Because you have hundreds of troops on the ground, the possibility of casualties and captured personnel is very high.” Given the limits of air power alone, experts said an airborne assault – similar to the one described in the CBS report – would be a necessary, if risky, way to counter Cuba’s military response. “What are we going to do? We're going to drop $100,000 bombs trying to go after insurgents in the mountains? Doesn't work that way,” Grazier said. “You need troops on the ground and you need a lot of them on the ground to be able to control territory.” If neither a blockade nor an air campaign with limited ground troops succeeded in forcing political concessions, the administration would be left with the last — and, according to every expert interviewed by Responsible Statecraft, the least attractive — option: a full-scale ground invasion.Experts said the opening phase of such an operation would move quickly. “Cuba has a tiny military, and it's not particularly capable,” said Grazier. “The green-on-green, U.S. regular soldiers up against Cuban regular soldiers – that part of the conflict would probably be very short.” But defeating Cuba's conventional military would likely be the easiest part of the campaign. The greater challenge, he argued, would begin after organized resistance collapsed. Cuba's military doctrine has long assumed it cannot defeat the United States in a conventional war. Instead, it emphasizes territorial defense and guerrilla warfare designed to make any occupation costly and prolonged.“This would be like the worst parts of Iraq and Afghanistan,” Grazier said, in which U.S. soldiers would be fighting against a “really hard to identify insurgency.”A large-scale invasion would also be difficult to conceal. Cancian said observers should watch for aircraft deploying to South Florida, naval forces assembling in the Caribbean, and additional Marines reinforcing the U.S. naval base at Guantánamo Bay. Those movements, he said, would likely precede any major military operation.
